y-m-77-01.title: Checking the numbers in a round-trip delivery speed report
y-m-77-01.topic: Average speed and the meaning of average
y-m-77-01.goal: Check by calculation that the average speed of a round trip may not equal the simple average of the two speeds, and say when they are equal.
y-m-77-01.material: A delivery driver made a round trip over a one-way distance of 12 km. On the way there, the driver went 30 km per hour, and on the way back, 20 km per hour (assume no stops and a constant speed on each leg). A coworker's report works it out as follows.
y-m-77-01.thinking.0: Find the line in the report that is skipped over without a reason
y-m-77-01.thinking.1: Check the value using the definitions of total distance and total time
y-m-77-01.thinking.2: Make several pairs of speeds that fit the conditions
y-m-77-01.prereq.0: In this task, 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty and support level in this production allocation. It does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume that high school vocational math is treated at an advanced difficulty, and that you already know middle-school-level ratios, percentages, averages, and expressions with letters.
y-m-77-01.prereq.1: Speed = distance ÷ time, the meaning of average (middle school level)
y-m-77-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in your coworker's work that lacks support or is wrong.
y-m-77-01.s.s1.line.0: Going: travel 12 km at 30 km per hour.
y-m-77-01.s.s1.line.1: Returning: come back 12 km at 20 km per hour.
y-m-77-01.s.s1.line.2: The average speed is the average of the two speeds, so (30+20)÷2 = 25 km/h.
y-m-77-01.s.s1.line.3: The round trip of 24 km can be made at 25 km per hour, so the time taken is 24÷25 = 0.96 hours.
y-m-77-01.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 simply copy the conditions, so they are correct. Line 3 is where the problem starts. Average speed is 'total distance ÷ total time', but even though the times for going and returning are different, the two speeds were averaged with equal weight. In fact, going takes 12÷30=0.4 hours and returning takes 12÷20=0.6 hours, so the whole trip takes 1 hour, and the average speed is 24÷1=24 km/h. Line 4 uses the 25 from line 3 as it is, which gives the wrong time of 0.96 hours. Whether you picked line 3 or line 4, you spotted a wrong line, but the cause is line 3.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the same road is traveled at a speed of a km per hour going and b km per hour returning. Make two different pairs (a, b) for which the average speed of the whole round trip (total distance ÷ total time) is a natural number. a and b are different natural numbers from 10 to 100, and the one-way distance does not matter. (30, 20) is already given as an example, so leave it out. (a, b) and (b, a) count as the same example.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.hint.0: Set the one-way distance to 12 km, and for each candidate (a, b), find the time going and the time returning and add them.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.hint.1: For several candidate pairs, organize in a table whether total distance divided by total time is a natural number, and look at what the pairs that give a natural number have in common.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are natural numbers from 10 to 100.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a and b natural numbers from 10 to 100.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The speeds going and returning must be different.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.ok.c3: This is a new pair of speeds.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.fail.c3: (30, 20) is already given as an example. Try to find a different pair.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.ok.c4: The average speed of the round trip is a natural number.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The average speed of the round trip is not a natural number. Calculate the total distance and the total time again.
y-m-77-01.s.s2.explain: For example, if the one-way distance is d, the time is d/a+d/b and the average speed is 2ab/(a+b). For (60, 40) it is 48, for (40, 10) it is 16, and for (60, 30) it is 40. Whichever pair you choose, the average speed is less than or equal to the simple average of the two speeds. It equals the simple average only when the two speeds are the same.
y-m-77-01.s.s3.prompt: Explain to your coworker 'why the average is not 25'. Use the times going and returning as your evidence, and add one sentence about whether there are cases where the simple average of the two speeds is correct.
y-m-77-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write the time going and the time returning as numbers.
y-m-77-01.s.s3.hint.1: Try starting with a sentence that compares the time calculated with 25 (0.96 hours) to the actual time taken.
y-m-77-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say in your own words that the times going and returning are different?
y-m-77-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give the value calculated from the total distance and total time as a number?
y-m-77-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state one condition for 'the cases where the simple average is correct'?
y-m-77-01.s.s3.model.0: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Going takes 12÷30=0.4 hours and returning takes 12÷20=0.6 hours, so it takes 1 hour in all, and since the driver went 24 km, it is 24 km/h. Returning is slower, so it takes longer, which is why it is not 25. The simple average is correct when the two speeds are the same, or when the times for the two legs are the same.
y-m-77-01.s.s3.model.1: If the driver had gone at 25, it should have taken 24÷25=0.96 hours, but it actually takes 0.4+0.6=1 hour. The time spent at the slower speed is longer, so the average is 24, which is less than 25. If the speeds going and returning were the same, the simple average would be correct.
y-m-77-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that gives the condition for the simple average to be correct only as 'when the speeds are the same' is also accepted.

y-m-77-03.title: Box packing cost: does one rule give the lowest price?
y-m-77-03.goal: Show by calculation that the rule 'use as many of the cheaper-per-item boxes as possible' does not guarantee the lowest cost for this order, and make several packing methods that satisfy the conditions.
y-m-77-03.material: A warehouse wants to ship 100 parts divided into two kinds of boxes. A large box (L) holds up to 12 parts and costs 1,500원 per box, and a small box (S) holds up to 8 parts and costs 1,100원 per box. Boxes may have empty spaces left, but all 100 parts must be packed. Any number of boxes may be used. One employee claimed the lowest cost like this.
y-m-77-03.thinking.0: Judging whether a rule (generalization) is valid
y-m-77-03.thinking.1: Making a packing combination that is a counterexample
y-m-77-03.thinking.2: Finding the conditions under which the rule definitely holds
y-m-77-03.prereq.0: In this task, 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty and support level in this production allocation. It does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume that high school vocational math is treated at an advanced difficulty, and that you already know middle-school-level ratios, percentages, averages, and expressions with letters.
y-m-77-03.prereq.1: Quotient and remainder in division, linear inequalities (middle school level)
y-m-77-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in the employee's claim that lacks support or is wrong.
y-m-77-03.s.s1.hint.0: First check by yourself whether the calculations in lines 1 and 3 are right.
y-m-77-03.s.s1.hint.1: Make several combinations that use fewer than 8 large boxes, check whether all 100 parts fit, and calculate the cost.
y-m-77-03.s.s1.line.0: A large box costs 1,500÷12 = 125원 per item, and a small box costs 1,100÷8 = 137.5원 per item.
y-m-77-03.s.s1.line.1: Therefore, using as many large boxes as possible is the cheapest.
y-m-77-03.s.s1.line.2: 100÷12 has a quotient of 8 and a remainder of 4, so use 8 large boxes (for 96 items) and 1 small box (for the remaining 4).
y-m-77-03.s.s1.line.3: The cost is 1,500×8 + 1,100×1 = 13,100원, and this is the lowest cost.
y-m-77-03.s.s1.explain: The per-item price calculation in line 1 and the quotient and remainder calculation in line 3 are correct. Line 2 generalizes 'it is cheaper per item, so use as many as possible' without a reason. In the method of line 3, one small box has 4 empty spaces, but if you use 7 large boxes and 2 small boxes, you fill exactly 84+16=100 items, and the cost is 10,500+2,200=12,700원. The 13,100원 in line 4 is not the lowest. Whether you picked line 2 or line 4, you spotted a wrong line.
y-m-77-03.s.s2.prompt: Using a large boxes and b small boxes, make packing combinations that hold 100 or more parts and are cheaper than the 13,100원 the employee mentioned. a and b are integers that are 0 or greater. Find two different combinations.
y-m-77-03.s.s2.hint.0: Change the number of large boxes a to 5, 6, 7, and 8, and find the minimum number of small boxes needed to hold 100 items.
y-m-77-03.s.s2.hint.1: For each candidate, write in a table whether the number of spaces is at least 100 and whether the cost is less than 13,100, and check.
y-m-77-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of boxes is an integer that is 0 or greater.
y-m-77-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of boxes must be an integer that is 0 or greater.
y-m-77-03.s.s2.fail.c2: This combination cannot hold 100 items. Count the spaces in the boxes again.
y-m-77-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The cost is 13,100원 or more. Look for a cheaper combination.
y-m-77-03.s.s2.explain: The only combinations that satisfy the conditions are (7, 2) and (5, 5). (7, 2) costs 12,700원 and has exactly 100 spaces. (5, 5) costs 7,500+5,500=13,000원 and has exactly 100 spaces. Neither has any empty space. The method of using 8 large boxes and putting the rest in a small box leaves 4 empty spaces in the last small box.
y-m-77-03.s.s3.prompt: For which order can you say for sure that the rule 'use as many of the cheaper-per-item boxes as possible, and put the remaining parts in a small box' gives the lowest cost? (The prices and sizes of the boxes stay the same.)
y-m-77-03.s.s3.hint.0: For each order, compare the cost of packing by the rule with the cost when you use one fewer large box and more small boxes.
y-m-77-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare orders where the rule leaves empty spaces with orders where it does not.
y-m-77-03.s.s3.r.a: Even with 98, 7 large boxes and 2 small boxes (12,700원) are cheaper than 8 large boxes and 1 small box (13,100원). This is an order where the rule breaks.
y-m-77-03.s.s3.r.b: The spaces fit exactly with large boxes alone, and no combination has a lower price per space than that, which is the basis.
y-m-77-03.s.s3.r.c: As you just checked, with 100 there is a combination cheaper than what the rule gives.
y-m-77-03.s.s3.o.d: It is so for every order, however many parts there are
y-m-77-03.s.s3.r.d: To say it holds for every order, you have to show there is no counterexample, but there is already the counterexample of 100.
y-m-77-03.s.s3.explain: 96 fit exactly in 8 large boxes, and the cost is 12,000원. For any combination, the price per space is at least 125원 and there must be at least 96 spaces, so the cost is at least 125×96=12,000원. So 12,000원 is the lowest. The rule is right for orders where the cheaper-per-item boxes alone fit exactly (multiples of 12), and for orders with a remainder you need to check.

y-m-77-05.title: When making a price list with a '25% margin', what should we ask first?
y-m-77-05.topic: The basis of the margin rate and setting the selling price
y-m-77-05.goal: Know that even the same percentage gives a different value depending on which quantity it is a ratio of, and write as questions the basis you should check before setting a price.
y-m-77-05.material: A stationery store wants to set the list price of an item whose cost is 8,000원. The team leader said, 'Please set the list price with a 25% margin.' Margin is the profit of the list price minus the cost (list price − cost), and ignore taxes and other expenses. Employee 가 said, 'Add 25% of the cost, so 8,000×1.25=10,000원.' Employee 나 said, 'The share of the margin in the list price has to be 25%, so if the list price is P, then (P−8,000)÷P=0.25, that is, P≈10,667원.'
y-m-77-05.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient and pointing out what is missing
y-m-77-05.thinking.1: Making cases where the value of a ratio changes depending on the base quantity
y-m-77-05.thinking.2: Writing a message asking the other person for the information needed
y-m-77-05.prereq.0: In this task, 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty and support level in this production allocation. It does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume that high school vocational math is treated at an advanced difficulty, and that you already know middle-school-level ratios, percentages, averages, and expressions with letters.
y-m-77-05.prereq.1: The meaning of percentages and ratios, solving linear equations (middle school level)
y-m-77-05.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting judgment about the two employees' calculations?
y-m-77-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write one line each for what 가 and 나 used the '25%' as a ratio of, and compare them.
y-m-77-05.s.s1.hint.1: Using each employee's list price, calculate margin ÷ cost and margin ÷ list price, and check which one comes to 25%.
y-m-77-05.s.s1.o.a: Employee 가's calculation is right. A percentage is multiplied by the cost and added, so 나's equation isn't needed
y-m-77-05.s.s1.r.a: You thought only in terms of the cost. You hadn't thought that the margin may also be stated as a ratio of the list price.
y-m-77-05.s.s1.o.b: Employee 나's calculation is right. The profit rate is always stated as a ratio of the list price, so 가's equation is wrong
y-m-77-05.s.s1.r.b: You thought only in terms of the list price. It is also common to state the margin rate as a ratio of the cost.
y-m-77-05.s.s1.o.c: If we set about 10,333원, the middle of the two values, it reflects both 가's and 나's calculations
y-m-77-05.s.s1.r.c: Mixing the two values gives a value that fits neither definition. The fact that the bases are different is not resolved.
y-m-77-05.s.s1.o.d: Both calculations are right. We need to ask the team leader what the 25% is a ratio of
y-m-77-05.s.s1.r.d: You recognized that the two calculations used different bases, and tried first to confirm which base it is.
y-m-77-05.s.s1.explain: 가 interpreted the margin rate as a ratio of the cost, and 나 as a ratio of the list price, and each calculation is right. 'A 25% margin' alone does not settle which base it is, so the list price is not decided as one value. If you pick one of the two at random, it may differ from what the team leader wants.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.prompt: The larger the difference between the list prices from the two interpretations, the larger the loss from a misunderstanding. When there is a cost of c원 and a margin rate of m%, make two different examples in which the difference between the list price based on cost (c×(1+m÷100)) and the list price based on list price (c÷(1−m÷100)) is 1,000원 or more. c is a natural number in units of 1,000원 (from 1,000 to 100,000), and m is a natural number from 5 to 50. The case of a cost of 8,000원 and a margin rate of 25% has a difference of about 667원, so it does not fit the conditions.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.hint.0: Keep the cost the same, change the margin rate to 10, 20, and 30, and make a table of the difference between the two list prices.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.hint.1: Keep the margin rate the same, double the cost, and check how the difference changes.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The cost is in units of 1,000원, from 1,000원 to 100,000원.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the cost in units of 1,000원, from 1,000 to 100,000.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The margin rate is a natural number from 5 to 50.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make the margin rate a natural number from 5 to 50.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The difference between the two list prices is 1,000원 or more.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The difference between the two list prices is less than 1,000원. Try changing the cost or the margin rate.
y-m-77-05.s.s2.explain: With a cost of 10,000원 and a margin rate of 30%, the list price based on cost is 13,000원 and the list price based on list price is about 14,286원, a difference of about 1,286원. With a cost of 20,000원 and a margin rate of 20%, they are 24,000원 and 25,000원, a difference of exactly 1,000원. The difference between the two list prices gets larger the larger the cost and the larger the margin rate.
y-m-77-05.s.s3.prompt: Write in one or two sentences a question to send to the team leader. It should include what you want to check, and why you can't decide on one price list if you don't know it.
y-m-77-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write in one word what changed between 가's and 나's calculations.
y-m-77-05.s.s3.hint.1: Put that one word in the blank of the frame '25% of ~' to make your question sentence.
y-m-77-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Team leader, the 25% margin is ...
y-m-77-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the question clearly ask 'what the 25% is of'?
y-m-77-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is it a question the team leader can answer in one sentence?
y-m-77-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you add the list price from each of the two bases as numbers?
y-m-77-05.s.s3.model.0: Is the 25% margin a ratio of the cost, or a ratio of the list price? On the cost basis it is 10,000원 and on the list price basis it is about 10,667원, so the list price differs depending on the basis and I can't decide the price list.
y-m-77-05.s.s3.model.1: Do you mean to add 25% to the cost, or do you mean the margin is 25% of the selling price? Depending on which, the list price differs by more than 600원, so I want to check first.
y-m-77-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that gives only the difference, without numbers, is also accepted.

y-m-77-06.title: Shift schedule: will there be days off together in the future?
y-m-77-06.topic: Schedules with different cycles and common days off
y-m-77-06.goal: Understand that listing a few dates and seeing no overlap does not let you conclude there will never be any, and find, explain, and fix the rule for a schedule in which two cycles never have a common day off.
y-m-77-06.material: Convenience store employee A takes a day off every 4 days, so rests on days 4, 8, 12, ... of the calendar. Employee B takes a day off every 6 days, and the first day off is day 1, so rests on days 1, 7, 13, 19, .... All days are counted from day 1, and assume the day-off rule continues for both people. Listing the days off of the two people up to day 25, there was not a single day they both rested.
y-m-77-06.thinking.0: Knowing the limits of generalizing from a few listed cases
y-m-77-06.thinking.1: Making a schedule with no shared days off by yourself
y-m-77-06.thinking.2: Explaining the reason with a rule and fixing it by changing just one entry
y-m-77-06.prereq.0: In this task, 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty and support level in this production allocation. It does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume that high school vocational math is treated at an advanced difficulty, and that you already know middle-school-level ratios, percentages, averages, and expressions with letters.
y-m-77-06.prereq.1: Multiples and divisors, the greatest common divisor, the meaning of remainder (middle school level)
y-m-77-06.s.s1.prompt: From the fact that they did not overlap up to day 25, can you say 'there will never be a day they rest together afterward either'?
y-m-77-06.s.s1.hint.0: List the days off of A and B up to day 40, and mark whether there is a day they share.
y-m-77-06.s.s1.hint.1: Write down what number the dates in the two lists share, and in what way, as a rule.
y-m-77-06.s.s1.explain: Even if the few cases you listed all give the same result, that is not evidence it will continue in the future. Whether there will be no overlapping day from now on is settled only when you explain it using the two day-off rules (multiples of 4, and every 6 days from day 1). Conversely, if even one overlapping day shows up, the claim that 'they don't overlap' is over.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.prompt: Suppose employee A rests every p days with the first day off on day f, and employee B rests every q days with the first day off on day g. Make two different schedules in which the two people never rest on the same day. p and q are natural numbers from 2 to 12, and the first day off is from 1 up to their own cycle (f is at most p, g is at most q). Schedules that swap A and B count as the same example.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a pair such as cycles 4 and 6, change the combination of first days off in many ways, list the days off up to day 40, and check whether they overlap.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.hint.1: When you get a schedule with no overlap, find and write down the property that all the days off in both lists have in common.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The cycles are natural numbers within the range of the conditions.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make p and q natural numbers from 2 to 12.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The first day off is within their own cycle.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The first day off must be at least 1 and at most their own cycle (f at most p, g at most q).
y-m-77-06.s.s2.ok.c3: In this schedule, the two people never rest on the same day.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.fail.c3: In this schedule, there will eventually be a day they rest together. Write the list of days off longer and look for the overlapping day.
y-m-77-06.s.s2.explain: For example, (4, 6, 4, 1) does not overlap because A rests only on even days and B rests only on odd days. In (6, 9, 3, 1), A's days off leave remainder 0 when divided by 3 and B's days off leave remainder 1 when divided by 3, so they cannot overlap. If the two cycles are coprime (having no common divisor other than 1, like 5 and 7), they are sure to overlap eventually. If the cycles have a common divisor greater than 1 and the first days off leave different remainders when divided by that common divisor, they do not overlap.
y-m-77-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain, using the properties of the two people's lists of days off, why A (every 4 days, starting from day 4) and B (every 6 days, starting from day 1) will not rest together in the future either, and write a way to make a shared day off by changing only B's first day off.
y-m-77-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: A's days off are ... and B's days off are ...
y-m-77-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly write what property applies to both lists?
y-m-77-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: After changing it, did you find and check one day they actually rest together?
y-m-77-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you look at which dates are possible for B's first day off (there are several)?
y-m-77-06.s.s3.model.0: A rests on multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, ...), so always on even days. B goes 1, 7, 13, ..., increasing by 6, so always on odd days. Even and odd can never be the same, so they can never rest together. If you change B's first day off to day 2, it becomes 2, 8, 14, ..., and they rest together on day 8.
y-m-77-06.s.s3.model.1: 4 and 6 are both divisible by 2, and A's days off leave remainder 0 when divided by 2 while B's days off leave remainder 1. So the same day can't come up. If you move B's first day off to day 4, they rest together right on day 4.
y-m-77-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: You may change the first day off to day 2, 4, or 6. If you change it to an odd number like 3, they still don't overlap.

y-m-77-07.title: The 'average monthly salary' in a job posting: can we trust it as it is?
y-m-77-07.topic: Mean, median, and reading data with a careful eye
y-m-77-07.goal: Know that an average can be pulled up by a few large values, make data sets with the same average but different distributions, and rewrite the wording so that a job seeker is not misled.
y-m-77-07.material: A small company's job posting says 'average monthly salary of 5 employees: 400만 원 (before tax)'. A job seeker who sees only this posting thinks that if they join, they will earn around 400만 원. The employees' monthly salaries are all whole numbers in units of 만 원, and each person's monthly salary is at least 200만 원.
y-m-77-07.thinking.0: Sorting out what cannot be known from the average alone
y-m-77-07.thinking.1: Making cases with the same average but different distributions
y-m-77-07.thinking.2: Changing the wording to suit the reader
y-m-77-07.prereq.0: In this task, 'H3' is only a label for the difficulty and support level in this production allocation. It does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this subject to a particular grade. Assume that high school vocational math is treated at an advanced difficulty, and that you already know middle-school-level ratios, percentages, averages, and expressions with letters.
y-m-77-07.prereq.1: The meaning of mean and median (middle school level)
y-m-77-07.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting statement about what the job seeker can judge from the posting's 'average monthly salary of 400만 원'?
y-m-77-07.s.s1.hint.0: Make two different sets of monthly salaries for 5 people whose total is 2,000, and check whether the averages are the same.
y-m-77-07.s.s1.hint.1: Make one of the two sets all similar values and the other with just one very large value, and compare the median values.
y-m-77-07.s.s1.o.a: It is an average that lets us assume most employees are paid around 400만 원
y-m-77-07.s.s1.r.a: You assumed that the average is near most of the values. An average is easily pulled by a few large or small values.
y-m-77-07.s.s1.o.b: The average alone does not tell the distribution, and other information such as the median is needed
y-m-77-07.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that data can differ even when the average is the same.
y-m-77-07.s.s1.o.c: We can assume at least one employee is paid exactly 400만 원
y-m-77-07.s.s1.r.c: You thought the average has to equal one actual value in the data. An average can differ from every person's monthly salary.
y-m-77-07.s.s1.o.d: It is an average from which we can be sure that more employees are paid less than 400만 원
y-m-77-07.s.s1.r.d: One average alone cannot settle that. There may be many people paid less, or few.
y-m-77-07.s.s1.explain: An average of 400 only means that the monthly salaries of the 5 people add up to 2,000, and it doesn't tell how they are divided. All 5 could be paid 400, and the average can also be 400 when 4 people are paid around 300 and one person is paid 800 or more. So you need more information such as the median or the lowest and highest values.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.prompt: Make two different sets of monthly salary data where the average is 400만 원 but only one employee is paid 400만 원 or more. Call the five monthly salaries, in order from lowest, a, b, c, d, e (만 원), and all are integers at least 200.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.hint.0: First set the highest monthly salary e to a large value like 500 or 800, and calculate what the sum of the other four people must be.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the monthly salaries of the other four are all less than 400, and if not, adjust the values.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The monthly salaries are integers at least 200.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The monthly salaries must all be integers at least 200.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.ok.c2: They are written from lowest to highest.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Please write a to e from lowest to highest (equal values are allowed).
y-m-77-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the five monthly salaries is not 2,000, so the average is not 400.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.ok.c4: Only e, one employee, is paid 400 or more.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.fail.c4: The fourth monthly salary d is 400 or more. Two or more employees are paid 400 or more.
y-m-77-07.s.s2.explain: For example, 250, 280, 300, 370, 800 add up to 2,000 so the average is 400, but the median is 300 and only one person is at 400 or more. 300, 300, 300, 300, 800 also has an average of 400. A single highest monthly salary can pull the average up a lot.
